John Barrett, United States minister to Panama, who has been minister to Siam and Argentina and commissioner general for the Louisiana Purchase exposition, had a unique experience during the late political campaign. While speaking in New England town he made the assertion that he knew well what it was to work on a farm.


A young farmer in the crowd, made skeptical by the speaker's faultless Prince Albert coat, immaculate shirt front, pale gray trousers and shining tie, shouted out, "You work on a farm? Bet yer never mixed a cow in your life!" "You take your hat," said Barrett, "I will put up $500 against the same amount that I can milk a cow faster than you can!"


This dare was accepted. The Democrats raised purse of $500 to match Barrett's $500 bill. Two cows were brought around. At the cry of "Ready, Go!" the milk ratcheted into the bottom of the pails, and Barrett's pail was full first, the meeting winding up in a blaze of glory.

Editor of The Times-Dispatch:

With dealing of limited education, can only judge results, and not explanation of results in other States that have passed through the long way. Road building is one and the same. The state of Massachusetts has then the best laws.

In brief, the Massachusetts highways are under State officers, and the state gives one-half and the county one-half, and the roads are built by contract, under the same safe contract act as a business man, and not by poll tax. In order to obtain the best result by this community of interest between the State and counties, they can afford to employ best experts to draw exact plans, specifications, etc. Here one county alone could not afford to do so. It takes the question out of county politics, which is the greatest giveaway of good roads now.

There are men in the Democratic party of our State who, as far as their fitness to the state is concerned, are dead; but unfortunately for good roads, they are not buried. There are many of us who are not dead, but had just as well be buried, so far as our fitness as citizens go. We do not attend to our own interests as citizens, and we cannot expect others to do so for us, except for pay or for political corruption, when we have not courage great enough to act for our own interests. We are bad citizens and no better than the politicians we abuse.

We must get into the fight in order to succeed, loaded for bear, expecting difference, prejudice, objections, etc. It is going to be a fight, and you or the elbow, it is going to come out on top, and who is the winner depends on training and organization. And if we have not grit enough to fight it out, we had best drop out now and not on the firing line. Millions of men go contrary to their best interest every day, and willfully, because they prefer to worship the dead idols of the past to the true and live gods of progress and system.

Pluck, grit and courage will win a touchdown in the game of good roads, and the fellows who kick hardest and last longest are the ones who will win. Is it going to be us or the other fellows?

Under present laws, as a owner of country and city property would not vote against the State or county taxing me more for spending one cent extra on roads, as most of the appropriations go into someone's pocket and the balance is injudiciously spent, resulting in bad roads.

At present, the road question is a political one and can only be won by electing good and true men to Richmond, those who are willing to serve at the request of their neighbors, at personal sacrifice, not that they want office, but who are willing to serve in order to protect their homes and residences against the waste that is going on under the present laws.

Personally, I will vote for a Democrat or a Republican if he is honest, and I do not care who you elect as President until I see our dear State take her form or position at the head of the sister States, as I am first, last and always for Virginia.

JNO. STEWART WALISE.
